propositions.text: The principal claimant and her children, Mexican citizens, claim refugee protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).
propositions.quote: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, the principal claimant, her adult children, XXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, and her minor son, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXX, who are Mexican citizens, are claiming refugee protection under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the principal claimant and her Mexican children claim refugee protection under IRPA sections 96 and 97(1).

propositions.text: The principal claimant is the designated representative for her minor child; the children base their claims on her claim.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant was appointed the designated representative for her minor child. The children are basing their claims on their mother's claim.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the principal claimant represents her minor child and the children base their claims on her claim.

propositions.text: The panel considered the Chairperson's guideline on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution under IRPA paragraph 159(1)(h).
propositions.quote: The panel took into consideration the Chairperson's guideline entitled Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution, pursuant to paragraph 159(1)(h) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the panel considered the Chairperson's guideline on women refugee claimants fearing gender-related persecution under IRPA.

propositions.text: The principal claimant fears persecutors who threatened her family while searching for her spouse in Canada.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant is afraid of XXXXXX, who threatened the members of her family. Those people had been searching for the principal claimant's spouse, XXXXXXXXXXXX, who was in Canada at the time.

propositions.text: Persecutors targeted the family because they could not find the spouse, so the claimant and children would be targeted if returned to Mexico.
propositions.quote: The persecutors, XXXXXX, had been unable to locate Mr. XXXXXXXX, and so they targeted his family as a way of finding him. Consequently, if they are forced to return to Mexico, the principal claimant and her three children would once again be targeted by those individuals, who had it in for Mr. XXXXXXXX.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimant fears persecutors who threatened her family searching for her spouse and would target them if returned to Mexico.

propositions.text: The spouse was found guilty under Article 1F(b) of the Convention for possession of marijuana over three kilograms for trafficking.
propositions.quote: She found that Mr. XXXXXXX was a person described in Article 1F(b) of the Convention, because he had been found in his car with XXXXX g of marijuana in his possession.

propositions.text: Trafficking and possession of marijuana over three kilograms is punishable by life imprisonment; spouse was arrested in 2000.
propositions.quote: In this case, and subject to sections 4 and 5, trafficking and possession of marijuana in an amount exceeding three kilograms for the purpose of trafficking is an offence punishable by a maximum sentence of life imprisonment. Mr. XXXXXXX was arrested in XXX 2000.

propositions.text: The panel did not believe the spouse's explanations and gave more weight to the guilty ruling information.
propositions.quote: The panel did not believe his explanations and attached more probative value to the information contained in the ruling that found him guilty.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found the spouse guilty under Article 1F(b) for marijuana trafficking and did not believe his explanations.

propositions.text: The claimant's problems began in 2008 when she received calls asking about her husband's whereabouts; husband told her to say nothing.
propositions.quote: According to the principal claimant's initial Personal Information Form (PIF), her problems began on XXXXXXX, 2008, at around 6:30 p.m., when she received a telephone call and was asked where her husband was. That same day, the principal claimant telephoned her husband, XXXXXXXX XXXXX, who was living in Montréal, and he told her to say nothing, because no one was to know where he was living.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimant's problems began in 2008 with calls about her husband, who told her to say nothing.

propositions.text: On the same day, the claimant was threatened and insulted by a caller demanding her husband's location and warned not to seek police help.
propositions.quote: On XXXXXXXX, 2008, the same person telephoned the principal claimant and again asked for her husband's whereabouts. Having received no reply other than that Mr. XXXXXXXX was no longer living there, the caller became angry with the principal claimant and insulted and threatened her, saying that she and her children might have a serious accident. He also stated he knew everything about her and her children, and he told her not to attempt to obtain the police's help, or she would regret it.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimant was threatened and warned not to seek police help when asked about her husband.

propositions.text: The claimant's husband told her to hide at a brother's home and said he would try to arrange for them to come to Canada.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant again telephoned her husband in Canada, and Mr. XXXXXXXX told her that she and the children had to leave the house and go into hiding at the home of a brother, XXX. Mr. XXXXXXXX added that he would look whether it would be possible for them to come to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the husband told the claimant to hide and that he would try to arrange their travel to Canada.

propositions.text: The claimant and children moved to a brother's house in Morelos; husband said they could travel to Canada, so she obtained passports and tickets.
propositions.quote: The next day, XXXXXXXX, 2008, the principal claimant and her children went to live at XXXX house in the city of XXXXXXX, in the state of Morelos. That same day, Mr. XXXXXXXX telephoned to say that the principal claimant and her children could travel to Canada, and that is why the principal claimant quickly took steps to obtain passports and buy the tickets.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimant moved to a brother's house and prepared to travel to Canada after husband's call.

propositions.text: Due to a wet passport, new arrangements were made; tickets were purchased and claimants traveled to Canada, filing refugee claims upon arrival.
propositions.quote: Because her son XXXX accidentally got his passport wet on XXXXX, 2008, the claimants had to make new arrangements to obtain this travel document. On XXXXXX, 2008, the principal claimant purchased airplane tickets to Canada. The claimants all travelled on XXXXXXXX, 2008, and filed refugee protection claims upon their arrival at the Trudeau airport that same day.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimants traveled to Canada and filed refugee claims after passport issues and ticket purchase.

propositions.text: On May 26, 2011, claimant added that armed men entered their home, beat her, threatened her and children, and warned against police contact.
propositions.quote: Significant additions were made to the PIFs on May 26, 2011. The principal claimant added that sometime around XXXXXXXX, at around 5:00 a.m., someone knocked at their door and her son opened it. Individuals entered their home and pointed a gun, asking to see the principal claimant's husband. She was beaten, and her children were terrified and screamed. Some neighbours came over. The assailants told the principal claimant that that would not save her, and they again ordered her not to contact the police, or they would kill her and her children.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimant added that armed men beat her and threatened her family, warning against police contact.

propositions.text: On May 6, 2011, claimant added spousal abuse allegations and that she filed a complaint but did not pursue police action.
propositions.quote: A second change to the narrative was submitted on May 6, 2011, when the principal claimant added, in the last four paragraphs, that she had suffered physical and psychological abuse at the hands of her husband. The principal claimant stated that she had filed a complaint in Mexico with the DIF, which suggested that she go and file a complaint with the police. She had refused to pursue this course of action any further.

propositions.text: Her husband did not appear when notified by authorities; he was arrested for spousal abuse in Canada and trial scheduled.
propositions.quote: Her husband did not appear when notified by the authorities, and the latter had told the principal claimant that her husband would be arrested if he did not appear. In Canada, the principal claimant found the courage to leave her husband. XXXX was arrested for spousal abuse and released on bail on XXXXXXX, 2011. His trial hearing is scheduled for XXXXXXX, 2012.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimant added spousal abuse allegations and that her husband was arrested and trial scheduled.

propositions.text: The claimants' identity was established by photocopies of their Mexican passports to the panel's satisfaction.
propositions.quote: The identity of the claimants was established to the panel's satisfaction by means of photocopies of their Mexican passports.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimants' identity was established by Mexican passport photocopies.

propositions.text: The determinative issues are credibility and state protection.
propositions.quote: The determinative issues are credibility and state protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the determinative issues are credibility and state protection.

propositions.text: At the hearing start, the principal claimant confirmed the PIF content was complete, true and correct.
propositions.quote: At the start of the hearing, the principal claimant confirmed that the entire content of the PIF was complete, true and correct.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimant confirmed the PIF was complete, true and correct at hearing start.

propositions.text: Claimant was asked about omission of armed men incident in May 6, 2011 amendment; she blamed husband's assistant for omission.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant was asked to explain the omission in the amendment received on May 6, 2011, of the events that allegedly happened on XXXXXXXX, 2008. ... The principal claimant blamed Mr. XXXX assistant, XXXXXXXXXX.

propositions.text: Claimant said no written copy of original Spanish PIF existed; amendment was produced about eight days after IRB decision on spouse.
propositions.quote: When asked whether she had kept a copy of the original Spanish version of the PIF, the principal claimant stated that it was not in writing. The panel notes that this amendment was produced approximately eight days after the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) decision's concerning XXXXXXXXXXX was rendered.

propositions.text: The panel does not accept blaming assistant as explanation; this undermines claimant's credibility on this testimony aspect.
propositions.quote: The panel does not accept that blaming Ms. XXXXXX constitutes an explanation. This undermines the principal claimant's credibility on this aspect of her testimony.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant's explanation blaming assistant for omission is not accepted and undermines credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant added that husband was a heavy drinker who beat her and that she attended a spousal abuse group meeting.
propositions.quote: Significant additions were also made to the PIF on May 26, 2011: the principal claimant mentioned that XXXX was a heavy drinker and that he used to beat her. The principal claimant added that when XXXX went to prison, the principal claimant's brother allegedly invited her to a group meeting where she talked about matters related to spousal abuse.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimant added that her husband was a heavy drinker who beat her and she attended a spousal abuse group meeting.

propositions.text: Claimant testified she left husband after abuse, rented a house, but returned after four months; problems calmed after kidnapping issues.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant testified that one day, XXXX beat her and she decided to leave him. She allegedly left and rented a house with the children, but four months later, she returned to live with XXXX. Things apparently calmed down with XXXX, but this was after they had the problems related to XXXX kidnapping.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the claimant left husband after abuse but returned after four months; problems calmed after kidnapping issues.

propositions.text: The claimant did not mention spousal abuse in initial PIF; panel believes it was added to embellish story, undermining credibility.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant did not mention spousal abuse in the initial PIF. The panel is of the opinion that this fact was added to embellish her story. This undermines the principal claimant's credibility on this aspect of her testimony.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the spousal abuse allegation was added later to embellish the story, undermining credibility.

propositions.text: Claimant spoke of death threat in 2008 omitted from narrative; she said stress caused omission.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant spoke of a death threat made on XXXXXXXXX, 2008, when the persecutors supposedly told her that they had confined XXXX and that he had escaped that night. When asked why this fact was omitted in the narrative, the principal claimant replied: [translation] "I didn't say it, I was under a lot of stress."

propositions.text: The panel does not accept stress explanation for omission; this undermines claimant's credibility on this testimony aspect.
propositions.quote: The panel does not accept that explanation. This undermines the principal claimant's credibility on this aspect of her testimony.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant's stress explanation for omitting a death threat is not accepted and undermines credibility.

propositions.text: The panel does not believe the principal claimant or her story.
propositions.quote: In short, the panel does not believe the principal claimant or her story.

paragraphs.summary: The panel does not believe the principal claimant or her story, the court finds.

propositions.text: Even if the principal claimant were credible, the issue of state protection remains.
propositions.quote: Even if the principal claimant were credible, the issue of state protection remains.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that even if the claimant were credible, state protection remains an issue.

propositions.text: Except in complete state breakdown, assume state can protect its citizens.
propositions.quote: Except in situations of complete breakdown of the state apparatus, it should be assumed that the state is capable of protecting its citizens.

propositions.text: International protection applies only when claimant has no other recourse.
propositions.quote: The presumption that the state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a claimant has no other recourse available.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the law that state protection is presumed unless state apparatus completely breaks down, and international protection applies only if no other recourse exists.

propositions.text: Claimant must provide clear and convincing evidence of state's inability to protect to rebut presumption.
propositions.quote: To rebut the presumption of state protection, a refugee protection claimant must provide clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect.

propositions.text: Evidence must be reliable, probative, and satisfy Board on balance of probabilities that protection is inadequate.
propositions.quote: The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, but must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.

propositions.text: Panel is not satisfied on balance of probabilities that state protection is inadequate in this case.
propositions.quote: In this case, the panel is not satisfied on a balance of probabilities.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the evidentiary standard to rebut state protection presumption and finds it not met here.

propositions.text: Burden of proof on claimant is proportional to democracy level of state; more democratic means claimant must exhaust more options.
propositions.quote: The burden of proof on the claimant is directly proportional to the level of the democracy in the state in question. The more democratic the state's institutions, the more the claimant must have done to exhaust all courses of action open to him.

paragraphs.summary: The court states burden of proof depends on state's democracy level; more democracy means claimant must exhaust more options.

propositions.text: Claimant must show all reasonable steps taken to seek protection, considering country context and interactions with authorities.
propositions.quote: The refugee protection claimant must demonstrate that he has taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the steps taken and the claimant's interactions with the authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The court states claimant must demonstrate taking all reasonable steps to seek protection considering context and interactions.

propositions.text: Failure to pursue state protection usually fatal to claim if state is functioning democracy with protection apparatus.
propositions.quote: In the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection within the country of origin will usually be fatal to a refugee claim-at least where the state is a functioning democracy with a willingness and the apparatus necessary to provide a measure of protection to its citizens.

paragraphs.summary: The court states failure to pursue state protection usually fatal to claim if state is functioning democracy with protection.

propositions.text: Principal claimant did not file police complaint, orally or in writing, citing fear as reason.
propositions.quote: In this case, the principal claimant did not file a complaint with the police, either orally or in writing. The reason she gave was the fact that she was afraid.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant did not file a police complaint due to fear.

propositions.text: DIF asked claimant if she wanted legal proceedings; she declined but had therapy once or twice, saying she no longer trusts authorities.
propositions.quote: The DIF, the state's public agency providing family services to which the principal claimant turned, asked her whether she wanted to initiate legal proceedings. The principal claimant did not want to go take such action, although she did undergo therapy once or twice. She explained: [translation] "I no longer trust the authorities."

paragraphs.summary: The court finds claimant declined legal proceedings despite DIF inquiry, had therapy, and no longer trusts authorities.

propositions.text: Adequacy of state protection cannot rest on claimant's subjective fear alone.
propositions.quote: The adequacy of state protection cannot rest on a claimant's subjective fear.

propositions.text: Claimant cannot rebut presumption of state protection by subjective reluctance to engage state in functioning democracy.
propositions.quote: A refugee protection claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy simply by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state in providing protection.

propositions.text: No state guarantees perfect protection; adequate protection is the standard.
propositions.quote: No state can guarantee perfect protection. Adequate protection is the standard to be satisfied.

paragraphs.summary: The court states adequacy of state protection cannot rely on claimant's subjective fear; adequate protection, not perfect, is required.

propositions.text: Panel reviewed and adopts reasoning of RPD decision TA6-07453 on state protection availability.
propositions.quote: The panel has reviewed the reasons for the persuasive decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) in file number TA6-07453, dated November 26, 2007, and adopts its line of reasoning on the availability of state protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court adopts reasoning of prior RPD decision TA6-07453 on state protection availability.

propositions.text: Principal claimant has not rebutted presumption of state protection in this case.
propositions.quote: The principal claimant has not rebutted the presumption of state protection in the circumstances of this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the claimant has not rebutted the presumption of state protection here.

propositions.text: The panel determines the named persons are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The panel determines that XXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX and XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX are neither "Convention refugees" nor "persons in need of protection."

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the named persons are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

propositions.text: Their claim for refugee protection is rejected.
propositions.quote: Their claim for refugee protection is rejected.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects their claim for refugee protection.
